title: The Hidden Code That Almost Sank GTA
lines: In 2005, a few lines of hidden code inside a video game got it pulled from store shelves, sparked a government investigation, and cost its makers millions. And that code was never supposed to be found.
The game was Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, the best-selling game on the PlayStation 2. The secret had a strange name. Hot Coffee.
So how did a few lines of locked code nearly take down Rockstar? It started with one curious fan in the Netherlands.
June 2005. A Dutch modder named Patrick Wildenborg is digging through the game's PC files. He finds a scene that was cut from the game, but never deleted.
It was an unfinished, adults-only mini-game. Rockstar had switched it off, but left it sitting on every single disc.
In the story, a girlfriend invites the hero inside for coffee. So fans called the unlocked scene Hot Coffee. Within days, it was everywhere.
At first, Rockstar blamed hackers, suggesting the content was made by modders, not by them.
But then players found the same scene on the PlayStation 2 discs, using a simple cheat device. And you can't mod a disc that's already in the box.
July 2005. The game's rating jumps from Mature to Adults Only. Overnight, America's biggest retailers pull it from their shelves.
Senator Hillary Clinton calls for a federal investigation, and the Federal Trade Commission opens one.
Copies are pulled and sent back. Lawsuits pile up, including one from an 85-year-old grandmother who bought the game for her teenage grandson.
So how did it all end? Not the way you'd think.
A class-action settlement offered buyers up to $35 each. Only a few thousand people ever bothered to claim it.
The FTC settled without a fine, but with a warning: hide anything like this again, and the penalties would be steep.
And the rules changed for good. Today, game makers must disclose everything on the disc, even content players can't reach. The re-released game went on to sell more than 27 million copies.
